title: Claims against the government, cities, police and public bodies

items.title: Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, 2019
items.says: This Ontario law sets the rules for suing the Ontario government (the Crown): when it can be held responsible, what immunities protect it, the notice that must come first, and how the case runs. It binds the Crown.

source.expect: This Act binds the Crown

items.title: The old Proceedings Against the Crown Act (history only)
items.says: The Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, 2019 replaced the Proceedings Against the Crown Act. The old Act still governs cases that were started against the Crown before the new Act came into force. Any case started now follows the 2019 Act, no matter when the facts happened.

source.expect: the Proceedings Against the Crown Act, as it read immediately

items.title: 2019 Act applies to cases started after it came in
items.says: The 2019 Act applies to every proceeding started against the Crown, or a Crown officer, employee or agent, after it came into force, regardless of when the facts took place.

source.expect: regardless of when the facts

items.title: Which law wins if two laws limit Crown liability
items.says: If this Act conflicts with another Act, this Act wins. But if another Act limits the liability of the Crown or its staff, whichever law gives the Crown more protection applies, unless that other Act says otherwise.

source.expect: greater protection against such liability prevails

items.title: Claims under special Acts are not changed
items.says: The Act does not change, and gives way to, certain special laws, including the Expropriations Act, the Public Transportation and Highway Improvement Act, the Land Titles Assurance Fund rules, the Motor Vehicle Accident Claims Act, the Workplace Safety and Insurance Act, 1997, and tax statutes. Claims under those laws follow their own rules.

source.expect: This Act does not affect and is subject to

items.title: A statutory right only works against the Crown if that law binds the Crown
items.says: A right given by another Act cannot be enforced against the Crown under this Act if the Act that gives the right does not bind the Crown.

source.expect: if the Act that confers the right does not bind the Crown

items.title: Municipal Act, 2001
items.says: The Municipal Act, 2001 governs Ontario municipalities other than Toronto. It sets out a municipality's duty to repair roads and bridges, the 10-day notice for road-repair claims, the protection for staff who act in good faith, and the court's power to cancel an illegal by-law.

source.expect: keep it in a state of repair that is reasonable

items.title: City of Toronto Act, 2006
items.says: For the City of Toronto, the City of Toronto Act, 2006 sets out the same road and bridge repair duty, the sidewalk snow-and-ice rule and the 10-day notice that the Municipal Act sets for other municipalities.

source.expect: The City shall keep a highway or bridge

items.title: Community Safety and Policing Act, 2019
items.says: This Act governs policing in Ontario. It makes police service boards responsible for the conduct of their officers on the job, and sets up the public complaints process run by the Law Enforcement Complaints Agency.

source.expect: A police service board is liable for the acts or omissions

items.title: Judicial Review Procedure Act
items.says: This Act lets a person ask a court to review a decision made under a statutory power, for example by a government official, a tribunal or a municipal body, and to set it aside if it was made unlawfully or unfairly.

source.citation: Judicial Review Procedure Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. J.1
source.expect: application for judicial review

items.title: Statutory Powers Procedure Act
items.says: This Act sets minimum hearing rules for Ontario tribunals that must hold a hearing before deciding: notice, the right to present evidence and cross-examine, and written decisions.

source.expect: an opportunity for a hearing before making a decision

items.title: Ombudsman Act
items.says: The Ombudsman of Ontario is an independent officer of the Legislature who investigates complaints about the administration of provincial government bodies and, since 2016, municipalities, school boards and universities.

source.citation: Ombudsman Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. O.6
source.expect: investigate any decision or recommendation made or any act done or omitted

items.title: Limitations Act, 2002
items.says: Most claims against the government, cities and police have the same basic time limit as any other claim: two years from the day the claim was discovered.

source.expect: after the second anniversary of the day on which the claim was discovered

items.title: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1)
items.says: Anyone whose Charter rights were infringed or denied may apply to a court of competent jurisdiction for the remedy the court considers appropriate and just. Damages are one possible remedy.

source.expect: such remedy as the court considers appropriate and just

items.title: Crown Liability and Proceedings Act (Canada)
items.says: Claims against the federal government (for example the RCMP, Canada Border Services Agency or Correctional Service Canada) fall under the federal Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, not the Ontario Act. The federal Crown is liable for torts committed by its servants as if it were a person.

source.citation: Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-50
source.expect: The Crown is liable for the damages for which

items.title: Ministry of the Attorney General Act, s. 8
items.says: A person who was prosecuted cannot sue the Crown Attorney or provincial prosecutor personally for what they did in the prosecution. The claim is brought against the Attorney General of Ontario instead.

source.expect: No action or other proceeding for damages shall be commenced by

items.title: Victims' Bill of Rights, 1995 creates no right to sue
items.says: The Victims' Bill of Rights, 1995 sets out principles for how victims of crime are to be treated by justice officials. It states that no new cause of action, appeal, claim or other remedy comes from those principles.

source.expect: No new cause of action, right of appeal, claim or other remedy

items.title: Canadian Victims Bill of Rights creates no right to damages
items.says: The federal Canadian Victims Bill of Rights gives victims rights to information, protection and participation, but says no cause of action or right to damages arises when one of those rights is breached. Its remedy is a complaint to the federal department or agency involved.

source.expect: No cause of action or right to damages arises

items.title: Special Investigations Unit Act, 2019
items.says: The Special Investigations Unit (SIU) is a civilian agency that investigates police and certain other officials when an incident involves death, serious injury, firearm discharge at a person, or an allegation of sexual assault. It decides whether criminal charges are laid; it does not award compensation.

source.citation: Special Investigations Unit Act, 2019, S.O. 2019, c. 1, Sched. 5
source.expect: serious injury

items.title: When the Ontario Crown is liable in tort
items.says: The Crown is liable in tort as if it were a person for: a tort committed by its officer, employee or agent; a breach of duty that comes with owning, occupying or controlling property; a breach of an employment duty owed to its own officers or employees; and liability under an Act, regulation or by-law.

source.expect: all the liabilities in tort to which it would be liable if it were a person

items.title: The Crown is liable only through the acts of its people
items.says: The Crown is not liable for a tort unless the tort comes from the acts or omissions of one of its officers, employees or agents.

source.expect: not attributable to the acts or omissions of an officer

items.title: If the employee is protected, so is the Crown
items.says: When a law protects a Crown officer, employee or agent from liability, the Crown gets the same protection. No claim may be brought against the Crown for an act if a tort claim for that act could not be brought against the officer, employee or agent.

source.expect: applies to the same extent and in the same manner with respect to the Crown

items.title: Contribution and indemnity apply to the Crown
items.says: The rules on sharing liability among wrongdoers (contribution and indemnity) apply to the Crown as if it were a person, so the Crown can be added as a party to share fault or can claim against others.

source.expect: enforceable by and against the Crown

items.title: Crown not liable for agencies, Crown corporations, funded bodies or contractors
items.says: The Crown is not liable for torts committed by Crown agencies, Crown corporations, transfer payment recipients (such as municipalities, hospitals, school boards, universities, children's aid societies and long-term care homes), or independent contractors. A claim about their conduct is brought against that body itself.

source.expect: The Crown is not liable for torts committed by

items.title: Who counts as a transfer payment recipient
items.says: A transfer payment recipient is anyone who receives provincial funding to deliver services to the public, including a municipality, a public or private hospital, a school board, a university or college, a children's aid society and a long-term care home.

source.expect: transfer payment recipient

items.title: Good-faith law enforcement and judicial acts
items.says: The Act does not make the Crown answerable for anything done in good faith to enforce the criminal law or the penal provisions of an Act, or for anything done by someone carrying out judicial duties or executing judicial process.

source.expect: anything done in good faith in the enforcement of the criminal

items.title: No negligence claim for making laws
items.says: No cause of action exists against the Crown or its staff for negligence in legislative work, such as preparing a bill, passing an Act or making a regulation.

source.expect: duties or functions of a legislative nature

items.title: No negligence claim for good-faith regulatory decisions
items.says: When a person is harmed by someone else who was regulated (for example licensed or inspected), no negligence claim lies against the Crown for a regulatory decision made in good faith, or for failing to make one.

source.expect: in respect of a regulatory decision made in good faith

items.title: No negligence claim for good-faith policy decisions
items.says: No negligence claim lies against the Crown for a decision made in good faith about a policy matter, or for failing to make one. Policy matters include designing, funding, delivering and ending programs. Common-law defences remain available too.

source.expect: in the making of a decision in good faith respecting a policy matter

items.title: What counts as a policy matter
items.says: A policy matter includes creating or changing a program and who is eligible for it, funding it or cutting its funding, how it is carried out (including by others) and how closely the Crown supervises it, and ending it.

source.expect: a policy matter includes

items.title: Barred claims are treated as dismissed
items.says: A proceeding about a matter covered by these immunities cannot be brought or continued, and is deemed dismissed without costs on the day the cause of action was extinguished.

source.expect: deemed to have been dismissed, without costs

items.title: Nelson (City) v. Marchi: policy versus operational decisions
items.says: The Supreme Court explained how to tell an immune core policy decision (based on social, economic and political factors, made in good faith and not irrational) from operational conduct, which can lead to negligence liability.

source.expect: economic, social and political factors

items.title: Cooper v. Hobart: when a public body owes a duty of care
items.says: The Supreme Court set out the test for a new duty of care in negligence: foreseeability and proximity between the parties, then any policy reasons to limit or deny the duty. It is often applied to regulators and public bodies.

source.expect: prima facie duty of care

items.title: No seizure of Crown property
items.says: No proceeding in rem may be brought against the Crown, and Crown property cannot be seized, attached, arrested, detained or sold.

source.expect: seizure, attachment, arrest, detention or sale of any property of the Crown

items.title: Notice of claim to the Crown at least 60 days before suing
items.says: Before starting any proceeding that claims damages against the Ontario Crown, the claimant must serve the Crown with a written notice of claim at least 60 days before the case is started. The notice must give enough detail to identify the occasion the claim arose from, and is served on the Crown Law Office (Civil Law).

source.expect: at least 60 days before the commencement of the proceeding

items.title: The Attorney General may ask for more details
items.says: After a notice of claim is served, the Attorney General may require more particulars needed to investigate the claim.

source.expect: may require such additional particulars

items.title: Limitation extended if the 60 days run past it
items.says: If the notice is served before the limitation period runs out, but the 60-day wait ends after it, the limitation period is extended to the end of the seventh day after the 60-day period ends.

source.expect: the last instant of the seventh day following the end of the 60-day period

items.title: 10-day notice for claims about Crown property
items.says: For a claim based on the Crown's duty as owner, occupier or controller of property (for example a fall in a government building), the notice of claim must be served no later than 10 days after the event.

source.expect: no later than 10 days after the occurrence of the event

items.title: No notice needed for a counterclaim or set-off
items.says: The notice requirement does not apply to a counterclaim, crossclaim or set-off against the Crown.

source.expect: does not apply with respect to a counterclaim, crossclaim

items.title: No notice means the claim is a nullity
items.says: If the required notice was not given, a proceeding brought without it is a nullity for that claim from the time it was brought.

source.expect: renders a proceeding brought without such notice a nullity

items.title: The Crown may settle a claim after notice
items.says: The Minister of Finance pays amounts the Crown owes under a settlement of a claim that was the subject of a notice of claim, or of an anticipated proceeding, as well as under final court orders.

source.expect: the subject of a notice of claim under section 18

items.title: How to name the Ontario government
items.says: In a court case, the Ontario Crown is named as "His Majesty the King in right of Ontario". A ministry is not named as a separate party.

source.expect: His Majesty the King in right of Ontario

items.title: Serving the Crown
items.says: A document that must be served personally on the Crown is served by leaving a copy with an employee at the Crown Law Office (Civil Law) of the Ministry of the Attorney General.

source.expect: Crown Law Office (Civil Law)

items.title: Serving the Crown in Small Claims Court
items.says: In Small Claims Court, personal service on the Ontario Crown is made in the way set out in section 15 of the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, 2019.

source.expect: in accordance with section 15

items.title: The usual court rules apply
items.says: Except where the Act says otherwise, the ordinary rules of court apply to a case against the Crown, and the court may make any order it could make between private persons.

source.expect: the rules of court apply with respect to a proceeding

items.title: No petition of right is needed
items.says: The old petition of right procedure is abolished. A claim against the Crown is brought as of right, as an ordinary proceeding, but limitation periods still apply.

source.expect: petition of right is abolished

items.title: Starting a Superior Court action: statement of claim
items.says: An action in the Superior Court of Justice starts with a statement of claim (Form 14A), issued by the court and then served on each defendant.

source.expect: is a statement of claim (Form 14A

items.title: Starting quickly with a notice of action
items.says: Where there is not enough time to prepare a statement of claim before a deadline, an action may be started with a notice of action (Form 14C), followed by a statement of claim (Form 14D) within 30 days.

source.expect: an action may be commenced by the issuing of a notice of action

items.title: Starting in Small Claims Court
items.says: A money claim up to the Small Claims Court limit (currently $50,000, not counting interest and costs) starts by filing a plaintiff's claim (Form 7A) with the clerk. Claims against the Crown, cities and police boards can be brought there.

source.expect: filing a plaintiff's claim (Form 7A)

items.title: Small Claims Court money limit
items.says: The Small Claims Court can hear claims for money up to $50,000, excluding interest and costs.

items.title: Defence due 20 days after service (Superior Court)
items.says: A defendant served in Ontario delivers a statement of defence (Form 18A) within 20 days after being served with the statement of claim.

source.expect: within twenty days after service of the statement of claim

items.title: Defence due 20 days after service (Small Claims)
items.says: In Small Claims Court, a defendant who disputes the claim serves and files a defence (Form 9A) within 20 days of being served.

source.expect: within 20 days of being served with the claim

items.title: No default judgment against the Crown without leave
items.says: The Crown cannot be noted in default, and default judgment cannot be entered against it, unless the court grants leave on a motion served on the Crown under section 15.

source.expect: except with leave of the court to be obtained on motion

items.title: Motion to strike a claim that discloses no cause of action
items.says: A party may ask a judge to strike out a pleading because it discloses no reasonable cause of action, or to decide a question of law before trial. Government defendants often use this step, for example to raise an immunity.

source.expect: discloses no reasonable cause of action

items.title: Summary judgment
items.says: The court grants summary judgment if there is no genuine issue requiring a trial on a claim or defence.

source.expect: no genuine issue requiring a trial

items.title: Hryniak v. Mauldin: summary judgment
items.says: The Supreme Court held that summary judgment is available where the judge can make the necessary findings of fact and apply the law, and it is a proportionate, quicker and less costly way to reach a just result.

source.expect: a fair and just determination on the merits

items.title: Discovery when the Crown is a party
items.says: The usual discovery rules apply to the Crown as if it were a corporation, with exceptions: the Crown may refuse to produce a document or answer a question on public-interest grounds; an official named by the Deputy Attorney General is examined; and the Crown delivers a signed list of documents instead of an affidavit of documents.

source.expect: in the same manner as if the Crown were a corporation

items.title: Public interest immunity
items.says: The Crown may withhold a document or refuse to answer a question where disclosure would be injurious to the public interest. The court can decide whether that claim holds.

source.expect: would be injurious to the public interest

items.title: No discovery of the Crown when it is not a party
items.says: The Act does not make the Crown or its staff subject to documentary discovery or examination for discovery in a case where the Crown is not a party.

source.expect: in a proceeding to which the Crown is not a party

items.title: Trial without a jury
items.says: A trial against the Crown, or against a Crown officer or employee, is heard by a judge alone, without a jury.

source.expect: trial shall be without a jury

items.title: No injunction or specific performance against the Crown
items.says: A court cannot grant an injunction or order specific performance against the Crown, or against an official where the effect would be relief against the Crown. Instead, the court may declare the parties' rights (but not by an interim declaration).

source.expect: grant an injunction or make an order for specific performance

items.title: A declaration of rights instead
items.says: In place of an injunction or specific performance, the court may make an order declaring the rights of the parties. It cannot make an interim or interlocutory declaration.

source.expect: make an order declaratory of the rights of the parties

items.title: Property claims: a declaration, not an order to return
items.says: Where a person claims property from the Crown, the court does not order it returned, but may declare that the person is entitled to the property or its possession.

source.expect: make an order declaring that the claimant is entitled

items.title: Limits on set-off and counterclaim against the Crown
items.says: A person sued by the Crown for taxes, duties or penalties cannot claim set-off or counterclaim. In other Crown proceedings, a set-off or counterclaim is allowed if it relates to a matter run by the same ministry.

source.expect: relates to a matter under the administration of the particular ministry

items.title: Costs
items.says: Costs are in the court's discretion. In a case where the Crown is a party, the Crown can be awarded costs and ordered to pay costs like any other party, including with offers to settle taken into account.

source.expect: in the discretion of the court

items.title: Offer to settle and its cost consequences
items.says: A plaintiff's written offer to settle made at least seven days before the hearing, which is not withdrawn and not accepted, can change the costs award if the plaintiff's judgment is as good as or better than the offer.

source.expect: at least seven days before the commencement of the hearing

items.title: Offer to settle in Small Claims Court
items.says: Any party may serve an offer to settle on another party, in writing.

source.expect: an offer to settle a claim on the terms specified

items.title: Settlement conference (Small Claims)
items.says: A settlement conference is held in every defended Small Claims Court action, before any trial.

source.expect: A settlement conference shall be held in every defended action

items.title: Discontinuing a claim
items.says: A plaintiff may discontinue all or part of an action against a defendant before the close of pleadings by serving and filing a notice of discontinuance (Form 23A); after that, leave of the court is needed.

source.expect: a notice of discontinuance (Form 23A)

items.title: Appeal
items.says: An appeal is started by serving a notice of appeal within 30 days after the order appealed from, unless a statute or the rules say otherwise.

source.expect: within 30 days after the making of the order appealed from

items.title: Interest on a judgment against the Crown
items.says: A judgment debt owed by or to the Crown carries interest the same way as one between private persons, and prejudgment interest can be claimed on money awarded.

source.expect: bears interest in the same way as a judgment debt

items.title: How the Crown pays a judgment
items.says: Apart from the garnishments allowed by subsections (2) and (3), no execution, attachment or similar process may be issued out of any court against the Crown.

source.expect: no execution or attachment or other process of a similar nature

review.problem: s. 27 (1) only bars execution against the Crown; payment by the Minister of Finance out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund is in s. 28, not the cited provision.

items.title: Payment from the Consolidated Revenue Fund
items.says: The Minister of Finance pays amounts the Crown owes under a final court order that is not subject to appeal, a settlement, or a final tribunal order or arbitration award.

source.expect: pay out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund

items.title: Garnishing money the Crown owes someone else
items.says: A garnishment may be issued against the Crown to catch money it owes a debtor for goods or services, or for support orders, subject to the Wages Act. It only reaches amounts payable by the ministry or unit that was served.

source.expect: A garnishment that is otherwise lawful may issue against the Crown

items.title: Claims of misfeasance or bad faith need leave
items.says: Section 17 applies to any claim against the Crown or a Crown officer or employee that includes misfeasance in public office or another tort based on bad faith in the use of public powers or duties.

source.expect: a tort of misfeasance in public office or a tort based on bad faith

items.title: Motion for leave to proceed; automatic stay
items.says: A case that includes such a claim can go ahead only with the court's leave. Until leave is granted, the whole case is treated as stayed from the moment it is started.

source.expect: may proceed only with leave of the court

items.title: What the claimant files on the leave motion
items.says: On the leave motion, the claimant serves on the defendant (on the Crown, under section 15) and files an affidavit setting out a concise statement of the material facts relied on, and an affidavit of documents listing all relevant documents the claimant has or had.

source.expect: a concise statement of the material facts on which the claimant intends to rely

items.title: The defendant may answer, but need not
items.says: The defendant may serve and file an affidavit with a concise statement of the facts it relies on for its defence, but it is not required to.

source.expect: but is not required to do so

items.title: Limits on cross-examination and discovery on the leave motion
items.says: On the leave motion, only the person who made an affidavit can be examined on it. The defendant is not subject to discovery, inspection of documents or examination for discovery for the motion.

source.expect: other than the maker of the affidavit or prescribed document

items.title: No discovery of the defendant on the leave motion
items.says: The defendant cannot be made to give documentary discovery or be examined for discovery in relation to the leave motion.

source.expect: shall not be subject to discovery or the inspection of documents

items.title: The test for leave
items.says: The court grants leave only if it is satisfied that the proceeding is brought in good faith and that there is a reasonable possibility the misfeasance or bad-faith claim would be resolved in the claimant's favour.

source.expect: there is a reasonable possibility that the claim described

items.title: Each side pays its own costs of the leave motion
items.says: Each party to the leave motion bears its own costs of that motion.

source.expect: shall bear its own costs of the motion

items.title: If leave is granted
items.says: Granting leave lifts the stay, and the case continues as an ordinary proceeding.

source.expect: lifts the stay of the proceeding

items.title: If leave is refused
items.says: If leave is not granted, the proceeding is a nullity. If the case also has other claims, only the misfeasance or bad-faith claim is a nullity, and the stay is lifted for the rest.

source.expect: the proceeding is rendered a nullity

items.title: The Crown may waive the leave requirement
items.says: The Crown may give the claimant written notice that it waives the need for leave, at any time before the leave motion is heard, even before a case is started. If it waives after the case starts, the stay is lifted once notice is given, and the Crown tells the court in writing.

source.expect: the Crown may waive the application of subsection (2)

items.title: When and how the waiver takes effect
items.says: The Crown may waive at any time before the leave motion is heard. If it does so after the case is started, the stay is lifted when the claimant receives notice, and the Crown must notify the court in writing.

source.expect: the stay of the proceeding is lifted once notice of the waiver

items.title: Leave not needed when the Crown is the claimant
items.says: Section 17 does not apply when the Crown itself is the claimant.

source.expect: This section does not apply if the claimant is the Crown

items.title: Older cases under the former section 17
items.says: Cases where a leave motion was brought before July 8, 2020 continue under the old version of section 17. Cases brought before that date without leave were a nullity for the misfeasance claim, but for limitation purposes count as started when they were brought.

source.expect: For the purposes of any applicable limitation period

items.title: Claim about a prosecutor is brought against the Attorney General
items.says: A person who was prosecuted and wants damages for something a Crown Attorney or provincial prosecutor did in the prosecution brings the case against the Attorney General of Ontario, who stands in the prosecutor's place and may be found liable instead.

source.expect: the Attorney General stands in the place of the person

items.title: Notice and procedure rules for claims against the Attorney General
items.says: The 60-day notice of claim, the limitation extension, the discovery rules, trial without a jury and payment rules of the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, 2019 apply to a claim against the Attorney General under section 8.

source.expect: subsections 18 (1) to (3) and sections 19, 20 and 28

items.title: Only claims that could have been brought against the prosecutor
items.says: A claim may be brought against the Attorney General under section 8 only if it could have been brought against the prosecutor but for the immunity.

source.expect: could have been brought against a person referred to

items.title: Misfeasance in public office: what must be shown
items.says: A claimant must show that a public officer engaged in deliberate and unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions, and was aware that the conduct was unlawful and apt to injure the claimant, plus the usual elements of any tort: the conduct caused the harm, and the harm is compensable.

source.expect: deliberate unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions

items.title: Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse
items.says: The Supreme Court described two forms of misfeasance in public office: conduct specifically meant to injure, and unlawful conduct done knowing it is unlawful and apt to injure. Both require deliberate unlawful conduct and awareness.

source.expect: deliberate and unlawful conduct in his or her capacity as a public officer

items.title: Malicious prosecution: the four elements
items.says: A claimant must prove the prosecution was (1) started by the defendant, (2) ended in the claimant's favour, (3) undertaken without reasonable and probable cause, and (4) motivated by malice or a main purpose other than carrying the law into effect.

source.expect: terminated in favour of the plaintiff

items.title: Nelles v. Ontario: no absolute immunity for prosecutors
items.says: The Supreme Court held that the Attorney General and Crown Attorneys are not absolutely immune from suits for malicious prosecution, and set out the four elements of the tort.

source.expect: There are four necessary elements which must be proved

items.title: Miazga v. Kvello Estate: malice means improper purpose
items.says: Starting a prosecution without reasonable and probable grounds is not enough on its own. Malice, meaning an improper purpose, must also be proved, and lack of a prosecutor's personal belief in the case is a factor but does not equal malice.

source.expect: requires proof that the defendant

items.title: Charter damages for wrongful non-disclosure by the Crown
items.says: A person who was prosecuted can claim Charter damages for wrongful non-disclosure without proving malice, by showing that (1) the prosecutor intentionally withheld information; (2) the prosecutor knew or ought reasonably to have known it was material to the defence and that withholding it would interfere with full answer and defence; (3) withholding it violated the person's Charter rights; and (4) the person suffered harm as a result.

source.decision: Henry v. British Columbia (Attorney General), 2015 SCC 24
source.expect: the prosecutor intentionally withheld information

items.title: Ontario (Attorney General) v. Clark: police officers cannot sue prosecutors
items.says: The Supreme Court held that prosecutorial immunity bars misfeasance claims brought by police officers against Crown prosecutors for decisions made in a prosecution. Claims by accused persons for malicious prosecution and wrongful non-disclosure remain available.

source.expect: whether prosecutorial immunity precludes misfeasance claims

items.title: Negligent investigation by police
items.says: Police owe a duty of care to a suspect they are investigating. Their conduct is measured against what a reasonable police officer would have done in similar circumstances, allowing for the discretion police work involves. The claimant also shows harm caused by the breach.

source.decision: Hill v. Hamilton-Wentworth Regional Police Services Board, 2007 SCC 41
source.expect: the police owe a duty of care in negligence to suspects

items.title: Hill: the standard of a reasonable officer
items.says: The standard of care is that of a reasonable police officer in similar circumstances, applied with recognition of the discretion inherent in police investigation.

source.decision: Hill v. Hamilton-Wentworth Regional Police Services Board, 2007 SCC 41
source.expect: a reasonable police officer in similar circumstances

items.title: Charter damages: the four steps
items.says: Damages for a Charter breach follow four steps: (1) a Charter right was breached; (2) damages would serve a purpose such as compensation, vindication of the right or deterring future breaches; (3) the government may show countervailing factors, such as other adequate remedies or good-governance concerns, that make damages inappropriate; (4) the court sets the amount.

source.expect: The first step in the inquiry is to establish that a Charter right has been breached

items.title: Ward: other remedies as a countervailing factor
items.says: If other remedies, such as a tort claim, already meet the need for compensation, vindication and deterrence, a further award of Charter damages may serve no function. The state bears the burden of showing such alternatives.

source.expect: a further award of damages under s. 24(1) would serve no function

items.title: Notice of constitutional question for Charter damages against government
items.says: Where a party claims a Charter s. 24(1) remedy for an act or omission of the Government of Canada or Ontario, or challenges a law's validity, notice must be served on the Attorney General of Canada and the Attorney General of Ontario. Without the notice, the remedy cannot be granted.

source.expect: A remedy is claimed under subsection 24 (1)

items.title: When the constitutional notice is due
items.says: The notice is served as soon as the need for it becomes known and at least 15 days before the day the question is argued, unless the court orders otherwise.

source.expect: at least fifteen days before the day on which the question

items.title: Form 4F: Notice of Constitutional Question
items.says: The notice of constitutional question required by section 109 of the Courts of Justice Act is in Form 4F.

source.expect: shall be in Form 4F

items.title: Antrim Truck Centre: injurious affection from public works
items.says: Where public works on land not taken from the owner interfere with the owner's use of land, compensation may be claimed under the Expropriations Act for injurious affection. The Supreme Court set the test for when the interference is unreasonable.

source.decision: Antrim Truck Centre Ltd. v. Ontario (Transportation), 2013 SCC 13
source.expect: must be both substantial and unreasonable

items.title: Municipal duty to repair roads and bridges
items.says: A municipality must keep its highways and bridges in a state of repair that is reasonable in the circumstances, including the character and location of the road. If it fails, it is liable for the damages that result, subject to the Negligence Act.

source.expect: liable for all damages any person sustains because of the default

items.title: Defences to a road-repair claim
items.says: A municipality is not liable if it did not know and could not reasonably have known about the state of repair, if it took reasonable steps to prevent the default, or if provincial minimum maintenance standards applied and were met.

source.expect: it took reasonable steps to prevent the default from arising

items.title: Minimum Maintenance Standards for Municipal Highways
items.says: A provincial regulation sets minimum standards for municipal roads, such as how often roads are patrolled and how quickly potholes and snow must be dealt with. Meeting these standards is a defence.

source.citation: O. Reg. 239/02, Minimum Maintenance Standards for Municipal Highways
source.expect: minimum standards

items.title: No claim for barriers or things beside the road
items.says: No action may be brought against a municipality for damage caused by the presence, absence or insufficiency of a wall, fence, rail or barrier, or by objects on or beside the untravelled part of a highway.

source.expect: the presence, absence or insufficiency of any wall, fence, rail

items.title: Snow and ice on sidewalks: gross negligence
items.says: A municipality is not liable for a personal injury caused by snow or ice on a sidewalk unless it was grossly negligent.

source.expect: Except in case of gross negligence

items.title: 10-day written notice to the municipal clerk
items.says: No action for damages for a road or bridge repair default can be brought unless, within 10 days after the injury, written notice of the claim and the injury, including the date, time and location, is served on or sent by registered mail to the clerk of the municipality (or each responsible municipality).

source.expect: within 10 days after the occurrence of the injury

items.title: No notice needed if the injured person died
items.says: Failing to give the 10-day notice does not bar the action if the injured person died as a result of the injury.

source.expect: in the case of the death of the injured person

items.title: Late or incomplete notice: reasonable excuse and no prejudice
items.says: Missing or insufficient notice does not bar the action if a judge finds there is a reasonable excuse and the municipality is not prejudiced in its defence.

source.expect: reasonable excuse for the want or the insufficiency of the notice

items.title: Not liable for others the municipality did not control
items.says: The road-repair section does not make a municipality responsible for someone acting under a legal power the municipality had no control over, unless it took part or the power was its own by-law, resolution or licence.

source.expect: over which the municipality had no control

items.title: A particular loss is required
items.says: A municipality is liable under the road-repair section only if the claimant suffered a particular loss beyond what everyone affected by the lack of repair suffered.

source.expect: a particular loss or damage beyond what is suffered

items.title: Councillors and staff not personally liable for road repair
items.says: No proceeding may be brought against a council member, officer or employee for damages based on the municipality's failure to repair a road, though contractors whose acts caused the damage can be sued.

source.expect: No proceeding shall be commenced against a member of council

items.title: Nuisance on a highway follows the same rules
items.says: The rules on untravelled portions, sidewalks, the 10-day notice and particular loss also apply to an action against a municipality for a nuisance on a highway.

source.expect: presence of any nuisance on a highway

items.title: Council members and staff protected for good-faith acts
items.says: No proceeding may be brought against a council member, officer, employee or agent of a municipality for acts done in good faith in performing duties under the Municipal Act or a by-law. The municipality itself remains liable for torts they commit.

source.expect: for any act done in good faith in the performance

items.title: The municipality stays liable for its staff's torts
items.says: The personal protection for council members and staff does not relieve the municipality of liability for torts they commit.

source.expect: does not relieve a municipality of liability

items.title: No nuisance claim for escaping water or sewage
items.says: No proceeding based on nuisance for water or sewage escaping from sewage or water works may be brought against a municipality, local board, or their members or staff. Claims in negligence are not barred by this section.

source.expect: in connection with the escape of water or sewage

items.title: No negligence claim for good-faith municipal policy decisions
items.says: No negligence proceeding may be brought against a municipality or local board, or their members or staff, where the action or inaction came from a policy decision made in a good-faith exercise of discretion.

source.expect: results from a policy decision of a municipality

items.title: Application to quash a municipal by-law
items.says: Any person may apply to the Superior Court of Justice to quash a municipal by-law, order or resolution, in whole or in part, for illegality. The application is generally made within one year after the by-law was passed.

source.expect: may quash a by-law of a municipality in whole or in part for illegality

items.title: One year to apply to quash a by-law
items.says: An application to quash a by-law, subject to section 415, is made within one year after the by-law was passed.

source.expect: within one year after the passing of the by-law

items.title: Complaint about an improperly closed council meeting
items.says: Any person may ask for an investigation of whether a council or local board properly closed a meeting to the public. It goes to the municipality's investigator, or to the Ontario Ombudsman if none was appointed.

source.expect: A person may request that an investigation

items.title: Toronto: 10-day notice to the city clerk
items.says: For a Toronto road or bridge repair claim, written notice of the claim and injury, including the date, time and location, must be served on or sent by registered mail to the city clerk within 10 days after the injury. Reasonable excuse without prejudice, or death, excuses missing notice.

source.expect: within 10 days after the occurrence of the injury

items.title: Toronto: late notice with reasonable excuse
items.says: For a claim about the City of Toronto's failure to keep a highway or bridge in repair, missing or insufficient notice does not bar the action if a judge finds a reasonable excuse and that the City is not prejudiced in its defence.

source.expect: the City is not prejudiced in its defence

review.problem: s. 42 (8) is limited to the notice required for claims about the City's failure to keep a highway or bridge in repair (s. 42); 'a Toronto claim' drops that condition and reads as if it covered any claim against the City.

items.title: Toronto: sidewalk snow and ice
items.says: The City of Toronto is not liable for a personal injury caused by snow or ice on a sidewalk except in case of gross negligence.

source.expect: Except in case of gross negligence, the City is not liable

items.title: Toronto: defences to road-repair claims
items.says: Toronto has the same defences as other municipalities: no actual or reasonable knowledge, reasonable steps taken, or minimum standards met.

source.expect: the City took reasonable steps to prevent the default

items.title: Toronto: council and staff protected for good-faith acts
items.says: No proceeding may be brought against a Toronto council member or City staff for good-faith acts done in their duties, but the City remains liable for their torts.

source.expect: for any act done in good faith in the performance

items.title: 60-day notice for snow and ice injuries on other premises
items.says: For a personal injury from snow or ice on premises (for example a municipal parking lot or a government building), no action may be brought against the occupier or its snow-removal contractor unless written notice, including the date, time and location, is served or sent by registered mail within 60 days after the injury. Public roads are governed by the Municipal Act instead.

source.expect: within 60 days after the occurrence of the injury

items.title: Occupiers' Liability Act does not cover public roads
items.says: The Occupiers' Liability Act binds the Crown, subject to the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, 2019, but does not apply to the Crown or a municipality as occupier of a public highway or road.

source.expect: occupier of a public highway or a public road

items.title: Police service board liable for its officers
items.says: A municipal police service board is liable for the acts or omissions of members of its police service committed in the course of their employment. The claim names the board, and the municipality is responsible for the board's liabilities.

source.expect: committed in the course of their employment

items.title: Municipality responsible for the board's liabilities
items.says: The municipality is responsible for liabilities the police service board incurs for its officers' conduct and for indemnifying their legal costs.

source.expect: The municipality is responsible for the liabilities incurred

items.title: Naming the police service board
items.says: A police service board may sue and be sued in its own name, so a claim is brought against the board (for example the "Ottawa Police Service Board"), usually together with the individual officers.

source.expect: may contract, sue and be sued in its own name

items.title: Board members protected for good-faith acts
items.says: Members of a police service board cannot be sued for good-faith acts done in their duties, but the board stays liable for its officers' acts as if they were its employees.

source.expect: does not relieve a police service board of liability

items.title: OPP officers: the Ontario Crown is liable
items.says: The Ontario Crown is liable for the acts or omissions of Ontario Provincial Police members in the course of their employment, so OPP claims are brought against the Crown and follow the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, 2019, including the 60-day notice.

source.expect: The Crown in right of Ontario is liable for the acts or omissions

items.title: Making a public complaint about a police officer
items.says: Any person may make a complaint to the Complaints Director of the Law Enforcement Complaints Agency (LECA) about the conduct of a police officer, a Niagara Parks special constable or a Legislative Protective Service peace officer. A complaint is not a lawsuit and does not award money.

source.expect: Any person may make a complaint to the Complaints Director

items.title: Law Enforcement Complaints Agency
items.says: The Law Enforcement Complaints Agency (formerly the OIPRD) receives, manages and oversees public complaints about police officers in Ontario, including municipal, regional and OPP officers.

source.expect: receiving, managing and overseeing public complaints

items.title: Complaints on behalf of others and through an agent
items.says: A parent or guardian may complain for a minor, and a substitute decision-maker for an incapable adult. A complainant may act through an agent.

source.expect: on behalf of

items.title: Complaints made to the wrong place are forwarded
items.says: If a complaint is made to the police chief, a police board, the Minister, the SIU or others listed, they must forward it to the Complaints Director and tell the complainant. It counts as made directly to the Complaints Director.

source.expect: shall forward the complaint to the Complaints Director

items.title: The Complaints Director screens the complaint
items.says: The Complaints Director reviews every complaint to decide whether it is about the conduct of a covered officer. If it is, the Director causes it to be investigated (unless refusing under section 158) and gives notice to the officer and the designated authority.

source.expect: shall, subject to section 158, cause the complaint to be investigated

items.title: Complaints more than six months after the events
items.says: The Complaints Director may refuse to investigate if the facts happened more than six months before the complaint. In deciding, the Director considers whether the complainant is a minor or has a disability, was facing a criminal investigation or charge about the events, and the public interest.

source.expect: more than six months before the complaint is made

items.title: Factors on a late complaint
items.says: For a complaint made after six months, the Complaints Director considers the complainant's age or disability, any criminal investigation or proceeding against the complainant about the events, and whether investigating is in the public interest.

source.expect: whether the complainant is or was subject to a criminal investigation

items.title: Other grounds to refuse a complaint
items.says: The Complaints Director may also refuse if the complainant was not directly affected (the person the conduct was aimed at, a person present who saw or heard it, or a close person who suffered loss from it), if the conduct is not misconduct on its face, or if the complaint is frivolous, vexatious, in bad faith, or not in the public interest. Written reasons are given.

source.expect: only the following persons shall be considered to have been affected

items.title: Who investigates the complaint
items.says: For a complaint about an officer below deputy chief, the Complaints Director usually directs the officer's own chief, or the chief of another police service, to investigate. The Director may keep the complaint and use LECA's own investigators if that is in the public interest.

source.expect: direct the officer's chief of police or the chief of police of an unrelated police service

items.title: Withdrawing a complaint
items.says: A complainant may withdraw on notice to the Complaints Director. The investigation then stops, unless the Director decides to continue in the public interest.

source.expect: a complainant may withdraw his or her complaint

items.title: Complaint paused for a criminal case
items.says: If the same matter is the subject of a criminal investigation or prosecution, the complaint investigation can be postponed or suspended so as not to interfere with it.

source.expect: may postpone the commencement of the investigation

items.title: Referral to the SIU
items.says: If the complaint may be a matter for the Special Investigations Unit, the Complaints Director notifies the SIU Director and tells the complainant; the complaint investigation is stayed while the SIU investigates.

source.expect: may be investigated by the SIU Director

items.title: Investigation target: 120 days, then updates every 30 days
items.says: The investigator aims to finish within 120 days, not counting time it is paused. After that, the complainant receives a status update every 30 days until it is done, unless that would prejudice the investigation.

source.expect: concluded within 120 days of its commencement

items.title: Written investigation report
items.says: At the end, a written report is prepared and a copy given to the complainant and the officer, once doing so will not interfere with any criminal investigation or prosecution.

source.expect: shall give a copy of the report to

items.title: Finding of no misconduct
items.says: If there are no reasonable grounds to believe the conduct was misconduct, written notice with reasons is given to the complainant and others.

source.expect: does not have reasonable grounds to believe

items.title: 30 days to ask LECA to review a chief's finding
items.says: Where a police chief investigated and found no misconduct, the complainant may apply to the Complaints Director for a review no later than 30 days after notice of the decision. The Director aims to complete the review within 60 days and may confirm, order a new investigation, or have LECA investigate.

source.expect: no later than 30 days after notice of the determination

items.title: What LECA can do on review
items.says: On review, the Complaints Director may confirm the decision, order a new investigation by the same or a different chief, have the matter investigated by a LECA investigator, or take other necessary action.

source.expect: confirm the determination

items.title: Finding of misconduct and discipline
items.says: If there are reasonable grounds to believe the conduct was misconduct, notice is given and the designated authority (usually the chief) decides on discipline and tells the complainant. For demotion or termination, a hearing before an adjudicator can be directed.

source.expect: impose the appropriate disciplinary measures

items.title: Adjudication hearing for serious discipline
items.says: Where demotion or termination may be the appropriate measure, the chief may apply for an adjudicator to hold a hearing.

source.expect: apply to the Commission Chair to appoint an adjudicator

items.title: Appeal of an adjudicator's decision
items.says: A party to an adjudication hearing may appeal the adjudicator's decision to the Divisional Court within 30 days of receiving notice of it.

source.expect: within 30 days of receiving notice of the adjudicator's decision

items.title: Informal resolution of a complaint
items.says: During an investigation the matter can be resolved informally, but only with the written consent of the complainant, the officer and the Complaints Director. Consent can be revoked within 12 business days.

source.expect: subject to the written consent of the complainant

items.title: 12 business days to revoke consent
items.says: The complainant or officer may revoke consent to an informal resolution by written notice no later than 12 business days after giving it.

source.expect: no later than 12 business days after the day

items.title: Informal resolution statements not usable in a lawsuit
items.says: Statements made while trying to resolve a complaint informally cannot be used in a civil proceeding without the consent of the person who made them.

source.expect: is admissible in a civil proceeding

items.title: If the officer resigns
items.says: If the officer resigns before the investigation report goes to the designated authority, the complaint process stops, but it can resume if the person is rehired as an officer within five years.

source.expect: no further action shall be taken under this Part

items.title: Judicial review of a LECA decision
items.says: A decision of the Complaints Director (for example refusing to investigate) has no appeal under the Act, but may be challenged by judicial review in the Divisional Court.

source.citation: Judicial Review Procedure Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. J.1
source.expect: application for judicial review

items.title: 30 days to apply for judicial review
items.says: An application for judicial review of a decision must be started no later than 30 days after the decision was made, unless another Act sets a different time. The court may extend the time if there are apparent grounds and no substantial prejudice from the delay.

source.citation: Judicial Review Procedure Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. J.1
source.expect: not later than 30 days after the date the decision was made

items.title: Extension of time for judicial review
items.says: The court may extend the 30-day time if it is satisfied there are apparent grounds for relief and no substantial prejudice or hardship will result from the delay.

source.citation: Judicial Review Procedure Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. J.1
source.expect: apparent grounds for relief

items.title: Starting judicial review in the Divisional Court
items.says: Judicial review is started by a notice of application to the Divisional Court in Form 68A. The registrar sets the hearing date.

source.expect: the notice of application shall be in Form 68A

items.title: Which court hears judicial review
items.says: Judicial review is heard by the Divisional Court. In urgent cases, with leave, a single judge of the Superior Court of Justice may hear it.

source.citation: Judicial Review Procedure Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. J.1
source.expect: shall be made to the Divisional Court

items.title: Interim order while judicial review is pending
items.says: On a judicial review application, the court may make any interim order it considers proper pending the final decision, such as a stay of the decision.

source.citation: Judicial Review Procedure Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. J.1
source.expect: make such interim order as it considers proper

items.title: Application record and factum within 30 days
items.says: The applicant delivers an application record and factum within 30 days after the tribunal's record is filed or, if no record is needed, within 30 days after starting the application.

source.expect: within thirty days after the record is filed

items.title: Certificate of perfection
items.says: The applicant files a certificate of perfection with the application record, stating that all required material has been filed and listing the parties' contact details.

source.expect: a certificate of perfection

items.title: Dismissal for delay
items.says: If the applicant does not deliver the record and factum on time or file the certificate of perfection, the respondent may move to the registrar, on 10 days' notice, to dismiss the application for delay.

source.expect: to have the application dismissed for delay

items.title: Judicial review does not automatically stay the decision
items.says: Starting judicial review is not an appeal, so the automatic stay that applies to tribunal appeals does not apply. A stay must be sought from the court.

source.expect: is not an appeal within the meaning of subsection (1)

items.title: Further appeal from the Divisional Court
items.says: An order of the Divisional Court may be appealed to the Court of Appeal on a question that is not a question of fact alone, only with leave of the Court of Appeal.

source.expect: with leave of the Court of Appeal

items.title: Right to reasonable notice of a tribunal hearing
items.says: Parties to a tribunal hearing must be given reasonable notice of it, and the notice states the statutory authority for the hearing.

source.expect: shall be given reasonable notice of the hearing

items.title: Hearing can go ahead if a party does not attend
items.says: If a party given proper notice of an oral hearing does not attend, the tribunal may proceed without them, and they are not entitled to further notice.

source.expect: the tribunal may proceed in the absence of the party

items.title: Right to present evidence and cross-examine
items.says: At an oral or electronic hearing, a party may call and examine witnesses, present evidence and submissions, and cross-examine witnesses as reasonably required.

source.expect: call and examine witnesses and present evidence and submissions

items.title: Written decision and reasons on request
items.says: A tribunal gives its final decision in writing, with written reasons if a party asks.

source.expect: shall give reasons in writing therefor if requested by a party

items.title: Asking a tribunal to review its own decision
items.says: If its rules allow, a tribunal may review all or part of its own decision and confirm, vary, suspend or cancel it.

source.expect: review all or part of its own decision or order

items.title: The tribunal's record of proceedings
items.says: A tribunal keeps a record of every proceeding in which a hearing was held, including the starting documents, notices, evidence and decision. This record goes to the court on judicial review.

source.expect: shall compile a record of any proceeding

items.title: A statutory appeal pauses the tribunal's decision
items.says: An appeal from a tribunal decision to a court generally operates as a stay, unless another law says otherwise or the tribunal or court orders otherwise.

source.expect: operates as a stay in the matter

items.title: Complaint to the Ombudsman of Ontario
items.says: A person may complain to the Ombudsman about a decision, recommendation, act or omission in the administration of a provincial body, municipality, school board or university. The Ombudsman investigates and makes recommendations; it does not award damages and its recommendations are not binding orders.

source.citation: Ombudsman Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. O.6
source.expect: in the course of the administration of a public sector body

items.title: Use available appeals first
items.says: The Ombudsman generally does not investigate where the person has a right of appeal or review on the merits to a court or tribunal until that right has been used or the time for it has passed.

source.citation: Ombudsman Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. O.6
source.expect: until after that right of appeal has been exercised

items.title: When the Ombudsman may decline
items.says: The Ombudsman may decline to investigate if, for example, the complainant knew of the matter more than 12 months before complaining, the complaint is trivial or not in good faith, or an adequate remedy exists.

source.citation: Ombudsman Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. O.6
source.expect: more than twelve months

items.title: Requesting provincial government records
items.says: A person may request access to records held by a provincial ministry or agency by a written request under the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act. Records can help prepare a claim.

source.citation: Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. F.31
source.expect: A person seeking access to a record shall

items.says: The institution generally gives written notice of whether access is granted within 30 days after receiving the request.

source.expect: within thirty days after the request is received

items.title: Appeal to the Information and Privacy Commissioner
items.says: A requester may appeal an access decision to the Information and Privacy Commissioner within 30 days after receiving notice of the decision.

source.citation: Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. F.31
source.expect: within thirty days after the notice was given

items.title: Requesting municipal and police records
items.says: Records held by a municipality or a police service board are requested under the Municipal Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, with similar 30-day timelines and appeals to the Commissioner.

source.citation: Municipal Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. M.56
source.expect: A person seeking access to a record shall

items.title: Two-year limitation period
items.says: Unless the Limitations Act provides otherwise, a proceeding cannot be started after the second anniversary of the day the claim was discovered.

source.expect: after the second anniversary of the day on which the claim was discovered

review.problem: Limitations Act s. 4 does not say it applies to claims against the Crown, municipalities and police boards.

items.title: When a claim is discovered
items.says: A claim is discovered on the earlier of the day the person knew, or a reasonable person in their circumstances ought to have known, that the injury happened, that it was caused by an act or omission, that it was the act of the person to be sued, and that a proceeding is an appropriate way to seek a remedy.

source.expect: a proceeding would be an appropriate means to seek to remedy it

items.title: Malicious prosecution: time runs once the prosecution ends
items.says: A claim is discovered on the earlier of the day the person knew, or a reasonable person in their circumstances ought to have known, that the injury, loss or damage occurred, that it was caused by an act or omission of the person to be sued, and that a proceeding is an appropriate way to remedy it. (The favourable-termination element of malicious prosecution needs its own source.)

source.expect: the injury, loss or damage had occurred

items.title: Time does not run while a person is incapable

source.expect: is incapable of commencing a proceeding in respect of the claim

items.title: 15-year ultimate limitation period
items.says: No proceeding may be started more than 15 years after the act or omission the claim is based on, whatever the discovery date, subject to exceptions.

source.expect: after the 15th anniversary of the day on which the act or omission

items.title: No limitation period for sexual assault

source.expect: a proceeding based on a sexual assault

items.title: No-limitation rule applies to old events

items.title: Other laws can change the time limit

items.title: No adding a defendant after the limitation runs out
items.says: Once the limitation period has expired against a person, the claim cannot be pursued by adding that person to an existing case, though a misnamed party can be corrected.

source.expect: shall not be pursued by adding the person as a party

items.title: Where to sue the federal Crown
items.says: A claim against the federal Crown may be brought in the Federal Court or in the superior court of the province (in Ontario, the Superior Court of Justice), which has concurrent jurisdiction.

source.citation: Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-50
source.expect: the superior court of the province

items.title: Naming and serving the federal Crown
items.says: A proceeding against the federal Crown is brought against the Attorney General of Canada, and is served on the Deputy Attorney General of Canada, as the federal Act and the court rules provide.

source.citation: Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-50
source.expect: the Attorney General of Canada

items.title: Limitation periods for federal Crown claims
items.says: For a claim against the federal Crown arising in Ontario, the provincial limitation rules (the Limitations Act, 2002) generally apply.

source.citation: Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-50
source.expect: the laws relating to prescription and the limitation of actions

items.title: Judicial review of federal decisions: 30 days
